outputs.L1:
A Creole boy, brought from the West Indies  
To gain the benefits of European learning,  
Was sent, some years before attending Westminster,  
To a preparatory school. From his artless tale,  
The mistress learned that he had not a single friend  
Upon English soil. As though she were his own mother,  
She made the dark Indian her particular care.  

Often she pondered her favourite’s future lot  
And sought to discover the bent of his young mind,  
For the kindly preceptress greatly wished to know  
Which profession he was most inclined to pursue,  
So that he might be trained wherever his genius led;  
For she believed that nature’s kindly bent was never vain.  

Yet all her efforts to discern his wishes failed:  
He continually evaded the repeated question.  
At last, one day, he came to her,  
Joy sparkling in his eyes, and declared  
That he wished to follow the same trade  
As those boys of colour who danced so happily  
In the open air.  

They were a troop of chimney-sweeping boys who,  
To wooden music and obstreperous noise,  
Dressed in tarnished finery and grotesque array,  
Were dancing through the streets on the first of May.
outputs.L2:
A Creole child from the West Indies was brought to England to receive a European education. Several years before he was due to attend Westminster, he was placed in a preparatory school. From his innocent account, the schoolmistress learned that he had no friends anywhere in England. She therefore took special responsibility for the dark-skinned Indian boy, caring for him almost as though she were his mother.

The kindly teacher often considered what his future might hold. Hoping to discover the natural direction of his youthful interests, she repeatedly asked which profession appealed to him most, so that he could be educated according to his abilities, for she believed that no inborn inclination was without purpose. Yet all her attempts to learn his wishes failed, since he continually avoided answering her questions.

At last, one day, he approached her with delight shining in his eyes. He announced that he wanted to follow the same occupation as the happy boys of colour he had seen dancing outdoors. They were a band of young chimney sweeps who, on the first of May, danced through the streets in faded finery and outlandish costumes, accompanied by clattering wooden music and a great deal of boisterous noise.
outputs.L3:
A young Creole boy from the West Indies was sent to England to receive a European education. Before entering Westminster School, he was placed in the care of a preparatory school. Since he had arrived in a foreign country without friends or family nearby, the schoolmistress took pity on him and treated him with the same warmth and affection she would have shown her own child.

Concerned about his future, she often asked what profession he would like to pursue. She hoped to identify his particular talents and natural inclinations so that his education could be shaped accordingly. For some time, however, the boy avoided giving her a definite answer.

One May Day, he suddenly approached her in great excitement and declared that he had finally chosen a trade. He wished, he said, to follow the same profession as the happy “boys of colour” he had seen dancing outside. The schoolmistress soon realized that he had encountered a festive group of chimney sweeps. Dressed in soot-darkened, tarnished costumes and noisily celebrating the holiday, they had appeared to him so cheerful that he mistook their merrymaking for evidence of an especially joyful and desirable occupation.
outputs.L4:
A young Creole boy from the West Indies is sent to England to be educated at a preparatory school. Far from home and unfamiliar with English customs, he is placed under the care of a kind schoolmistress who takes a special interest in him. She hopes to discover what sort of career would best match his abilities and temperament, and she repeatedly asks him what profession he would like to follow when he grows older. The boy, however, has little knowledge of English society or of the actual demands of its various occupations, so he cannot give her a definite answer.

One May Day, he sees a group of chimney sweeps taking part in the traditional festivities. Dressed for the celebration, dancing, and appearing merry and carefree, they make a powerful impression on him. He knows nothing of their usual lives—the soot, danger, exhaustion, poverty, and exploitation associated with chimney sweeping. He sees only their music, movement, and holiday cheer. When his schoolmistress once again asks him to choose a profession, he confidently declares that he would like to become a chimney sweep.

His answer is both comic and touching. The adults have tried to guide him toward a sensible future, but their questions assume a knowledge of the world that he does not yet possess. The boy chooses according to the most attractive image before him, mistaking a rare day of festivity for the ordinary reality of the trade. His decision reveals the innocence of childhood, the misunderstandings produced by cultural unfamiliarity, and the limits of adult attempts to shape a child’s destiny through abstract advice alone.
outputs.L5:
### Creole Culture in the West Indies

The West Indies are home to rich and diverse Creole cultures shaped by centuries of migration, colonization, slavery, resistance, and cultural exchange. Indigenous Caribbean traditions combined with African, European, and Asian influences to create distinctive languages, cuisines, music, religions, and social customs.

The word **Creole** has several meanings across the region. It can describe people born in the Caribbean, communities of mixed cultural heritage, or languages that developed through contact between different populations. Creole languages—such as Haitian Creole, Jamaican Patois, and the French-based Creoles of Martinique and Saint Lucia—reflect both the history and creativity of their speakers.

Creole identity is especially visible in West Indian food and music. Dishes often blend local ingredients with African cooking methods, European recipes, and Indian or Chinese spices. Musical traditions such as calypso, reggae, zouk, and soca similarly express the region’s complex history while celebrating community and resilience.

There is no single Creole culture shared by all the West Indies. Each island has its own traditions and understanding of the term. Together, however, these cultures demonstrate how Caribbean peoples transformed difficult historical circumstances into vibrant and enduring forms of expression.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem in rhyming couplets about a Creole schoolboy in England who mistakes May Day chimney sweeps for a desirable profession.
counterfactuals.output:
Young Lucien came from islands bright with cane,  
To board at school beneath the English rain.  

He missed the drums that warmed the harbor air,  
The mango scent, the salt wind in his hair.  

But on the first of May, at morning’s call,  
A troop of chimney sweeps danced past the wall.  

Their jackets shone with ribbons, red and green,  
Their faces blacked, their silver buckles clean.  

A fiddler played; a garland crowned the street;  
The laughing townsfolk tossed coins at their feet.  

Lucien cried, “At last, a trade of cheer—  
The finest work I’ve seen since coming here!  

“They dance all day, with flowers on each broom,  
And wake the spring from every wintered room.  

“They earn applause wherever they may go;  
I’ll be a sweep, and join their merry show!”  

He left his books and found their master’s door,  
Where soot lay thick on window, step, and floor.  

“Good sir,” he said, “I’ve come to learn your trade—  
To wear bright bows and lead the May parade.”  

The master laughed, then pointed to a grate:  
“Climb up that flue, and we shall test your fate.”  

One cough, one scrape, one shower dark as night—  
Lucien shot down, no ribbon left in sight.  

He staggered forth, a shadow of a boy,  
And asked, “Is this the daily part of joy?”  

“The dance,” the master said, “comes once a year;  
The rest is smoke, hard climbing, grime, and fear.”  

Lucien washed until the basin turned to ink,  
Then sat beside his schoolbooks, deep in think.  

Next May he cheered the sweeps who crossed the square,  
But chose a trade with sunlight, room, and air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an eighteenth-century-style verse about a compassionate schoolmistress trying to discover the vocational interests of a West Indian child.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the tamarind’s hospitable shade,  
A gentle dame her little school survey’d;  
To one young child of India’s western isles  
She bent her ear, and won his thought with smiles.  

“What future calling most delights thy breast—  
The merchant’s toil, the healing art’s behest?  
Wouldst thou brave seas, make fruitful gardens bloom,  
Build stately roofs, or ply the scholar’s room?”  

No choice she urg’d, nor check’d his modest tongue,  
But prais’d each hope, however faintly sprung;  
Till, warm’d by kindness, he at last confess’d:  
“To teach, like thee, would please my spirit best.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a satirical poem using archaic diction in which a boy sent to a preparatory school sees happy chimney sweeps celebrating May Day and chooses their trade.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Scholar and the Soot**

“Now hie thee hence,” the father cried,  
“Unto thy grammar-school,  
Where birch shall make thy manners meek,  
And Latin prove thee fool.  

“There shalt thou con thy *hic* and *haec*,  
Decline thy daily bread,  
And learn why noble Hannibal  
Was inconveniently dead.”  

The stripling sighed, and took the road,  
With satchel, slate, and dread;  
His hose were new, his collar starched,  
His heart was lumpen lead.  

But lo! upon the first of May,  
Beside the village green,  
A merry rout of chimney-boys  
In crowns of leaves was seen.  

Their visages were black as night,  
Their teeth like pearls did shine;  
They danced about a garland tall  
And quaffed the landlord’s wine.  

“Gramercy, lads!” the scholar cried,  
“What school hath made ye glad?  
What master grants this holiday  
And beats no trembling lad?”  

“No school have we,” the sweeps replied,  
“No Greek nor sums we know;  
We climb where learned doctors’ wits  
Would fear full sore to go.  

“Our copybook is roof and flue,  
Our ink the honest soot;  
Our rod’s a brush, our desk a grate,  
Our learning—hand and foot.  

“Though lords beneath us snore in silk,  
Above their heads we creep;  
And every man who calls us low  
Must pay us ere we sweep.”  

The boy cast down his grammar then,  
His rules, his slate, his pride:  
“By cock and pie, your trade is mine!  
Good fellows, stand aside.  

“Let pedants scourge the parts of speech,  
Let ushers rant till noon;  
I’d rather climb a duke’s foul stack  
And dance beneath the moon.”  

His father came at Michaelmas  
To hear the youth construe;  
He found him black from crown to heel,  
Yet richer by a sou.  

“Alas!” quoth he, “my gentle son,  
What ruin hath been wrought?”  
“Nay, sir,” the merry sweep replied,  
“I practise what I’m taught.  

“For schoolmen say we needs must rise  
If honour we would win;  
I rise each morn above the great—  
And cleanse their dirt within.”  

Then off he strode with brush in hand,  
A lord of pot and flue;  
Whilst through the schoolroom window wailed  
The sons who stayed—and knew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
